item.title: Could Haley Stevens cost Democrats the Senate?
item.description: Probably not, but let’s run the numbers on a rare *November* Surprise. Plus, please join us for our Election Night coverage!
item.content:encoded:
With 48 hours to go until votes begin to be counted on Tuesday night, I don’t really have time for anything other than full transparency. We’d planned to probably publish a second post today — please see our fun morning post with 13 quasi-randomly selected FLIPR maps — and this second post was originally slotted in as a relatively naked advertisement for our Election Night coverage, which we’ll be co-hosting with the good folks at The Argument, GD Politics and Slow Boring. If everything goes to plan, we’ll have both a (free) live video stream and a paid-subscribers-only liveblog.1 I’m mostly going to be focused on the liveblog component, but we’ll have plenty of insightful contributors for you on both channels.

I figured the post would start by talking about some of Sunday morning’s more interesting polls. But surprise #1: there weren’t many polls, nor were any of them all that interesting. Incentives in the industry are changing, and not necessarily in a good way. Sundays used to be big days for politics coverage back in the era of Sunday newspaper print editions and when shows like Meet the Press were incredibly influential. Now, the conventional wisdom seems to be that you fire out your best stuff on weekdays instead.2 Plus, high-quality polling is expensive, and pollsters may feel like they’re in a no-win position where they’ll either get accused of herding or risk publishing an outlier-ish poll that will surely get them criticized if they’re wrong — or who knows, maybe even sued by the president?

But then early this afternoon, we got a real surprise: Haley Stevens, whom Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated in the August Democratic primary for U.S. Senate, endorsed his Republican opponent Mike Rogers.

I’m going to be honest that I thought this was a fake headline when I first came across it on Twitter, sort of like I originally worried I might be hallucinating when I first heard about the Luka Doncic trade.3 I’m also going to be honest that I’ve sort of tuned out stories about the Democratic infighting in Michigan. Don’t get me wrong: we love talking about Democratic infighting at Silver Bulletin, love it, love it, love it. But it’s pretty much the only thing that anyone is going to be talking about in politics from early next year onward, when candidates begin to declare for the 2028 race, until the DNC in Boston, Denver, or Philadelphia in August 2028.

You can watch the Stevens video for yourself, but to me at least, she comes across as fairly petty and vindictive. To be fair, though, so has El-Sayed, who disinvited Stevens from campaign events. There’s not much maturity on display here. If Democrats had to do it over again, maybe they’d have nominated Mallory McMorrow, or begged Gary Peters to run for another term.

But could this actually swing the race?

Not that you should necessarily trust my instincts on this vibes-based stuff, but I’m of mixed minds here. Let’s start with the polls, where there’s good news and bad news for El-Sayed.

Good news for AES part #1a: he’s actually been expanding his lead over Rogers in recent surveys. Indeed, Michigan has been one of the better positive surprises for Democrats lately in polls that have mostly been fairly flat during the stretch run. Part #1b: he already has almost 50 percent of the vote. In fact, Michigan has among the fewest undecided voters4 of any Senate race at 4.8 percent; the lowest is Maine at 3.5 percent.

Now, polls can be wrong, of course. But even when they are wrong, it’s relatively uncommon for a candidate to finish with a lower share than their decided vote in the polls. Even Hillary Clinton didn’t do that: in 2016, she got 48.2 percent of the popular vote, versus 46.8 percent of the decided vote in the polls. (Donald Trump gained more ground, though still lost the popular vote.)

Indeed, FLIPR accounts for the number of undecideds. It’s a bit more confident about its forecasts when there are less of them, which is one of the reasons it’s had a pretty bullish forecast for El-Sayed.

Bad news for El-Sayed: look at the trajectory of the polls in that first chart. He was actually trailing Rogers back when he and Stevens were fighting in the summer before the primary was complete. So there’s at least some evidence that voters in Michigan are sensitive to Democratic unity, or the lack thereof.

To summarize my understanding of the impact of endorsements: the political science literature generally says endorsements aren’t that important unless they’re surprising, and this one was surprising. Or at least surprising-ish: tensions between the candidates had already been escalating and, as I wrote above, it hadn’t seemed to hurt El-Sayed in the polls; in fact, he was gaining ground.

There’s also the fact that roughly 1.9 million Michiganders have already voted, which might reflect something like 40 percent of the eventual turnout there, not counting voters whose ballots are in the mail but haven’t been counted yet. Now, generally speaking, undecided voters don’t vote early: rather, committed partisans do. But that blunts the effect, to some degree. It would probably have been worse for El-Sayed if this happened last weekend, in which case there would also have been more time for the story to metastasize in the national media. But now, newsroom resources are stretched thin as everyone prepares for Tuesday.

Even if this hurts El-Sayed with some voters, could it help him with others?

I won’t precisely share my Michigan mom’s reaction to hearing about the news today, but it did help to clarify one question for me. Are there any voters for whom this might reinforce support for AES?

I think it’s always important to ask this question when there is some sort of October/November Surprise. Let’s say that 3 percent of undecided voters5 are motivated to change their votes because of some breaking news, and they all move in the same direction — toward the Republican, say, after a late-breaking scandal involving the Democratic candidate. But suppose instead that, while 2 percent of those undecided voters lock in for the Republican, 1 percent move toward the Democrat instead. The net impact is now -1 instead of -3, only a third as much.

That might sound contrived, but take something like the Mary Peltola scandal in Alaska for reportedly being abusive to her staff. FLIPR now “officially” treats this as a scandal, even though it’s toward the lower wattage end as scandals go.

There are ways, though, that story might be read positively by an undecided voter in red Alaska. Peltola curses a lot, and she doesn’t have much patience for her overly sensitive, woke staffers, who complained about such things as being instructed to feed her chameleon.

Now, there is some legitimately bad behavior in the story too — she allegedly pushed a staffer. But there are probably some voters out there who read the story as a net positive. It sort of reinforces an image of Peltola being tough and not tolerating any bullshit. Indeed, you’d be hard-pressed to detect any net-negative fallout from it in Peltola’s polls:6

By contrast, take the FBI deciding to re-open an investigation into Hillary Clinton’s email server in late October, 2016. Maybe voters were going to care about that and maybe they weren’t. (Indeed, there’s good evidence that this did affect the race, maybe even decisively.) But nobody was going to think more positively about Clinton because of it. Indeed, some Democrats thought it actually hurt Clinton when she was eventually re-cleared simply because it recirculated the words “Clinton”, “FBI” and “email” in close proximity to one another in news headlines.

El-Sayed has been running against the Democratic establishment in Michigan, a state that has long had a penchant for anti-establishment, outsider candidates. Bernie Sanders won the state in 2016, Jesse Jackson did in 1988, and it was one of John McCain’s few wins against George W. Bush in 2000. Stevens famously became an avatar of the said establishment in a race where a major question was about AIPAC’s heavy spending on behalf of Stevens.

Then again, El-Sayed barely won that primary in what nearly was a massively wrong call by the polls. He’s frankly one of the weirder candidates we’ve seen in recent years: quite charismatic and very bro-y. But also he’s someone who can really get his back up instead of turning the other cheek. As someone who can be a bit confrontational myself, I sort of admire it in a weird way, but there’s a reason I’d never run for United States Senate. I don’t think there’s clear evidence on how this plays with voters; it would have been clearer if he’d won the primary by more.

Let’s turn to FLIPR

So let’s say the Stevens endorsement of Rogers reduces El-Sayed’s margin by 1 percentage point. If he’d been on track to win by 4 percent, now he’ll win by 3 instead, for instance. Or, if he was going to squeak by with an 0.5-percent victory, now he’ll lose by 0.5 points.

That 1-point swing is just an educated guess, and might be toward the higher side of my prior. Again: not many undecideds in Michigan, many people have already voted, the story might read positively for some voters, and many purported “game-changers” prove to be nothing of the sort. Weigh that against the fact that El-Sayed’s numbers did seem to suffer during the heat of the primary campaign in the summer. Let’s just stick with 1 percent.

How often, in FLIPR, did El-Sayed win Michigan by 1 point or less? In Saturday’s simulations, about 5 percent of the time. Again, AES does have some cushion in the polls. But if the polls are off, they might be so off that he was bound to lose anyway. It’s not quite that Rogers has to hit the bullseye, but it’s a pretty narrow target.

Next question: how often, in FLIPR’s simulations, did El-Sayed beat Rogers by less than 1 point and Democrats finish with exactly 51 Senate seats? In other words, a narrow win in Michigan that decided control of the Senate? That happened in 316 of our 40,000 simulations. So about 1 percent of the time, if you round up slightly.

(All of this is fairly linear, by the way. If you think the endorsement will hurt El-Sayed by half-a-point, the chances that it flips Michigan against him go down to about 2.5 percent, and the odds that it flips the Senate to 0.5 percent.)

So there’s a chance, indeed, that Haley Stevens just cost Democrats the Senate. It’s just not particularly high, unless your estimate of the endorsement’s importance is higher than mine.

This will complicate interpretations of Michigan, and not in a way that helps centrists

But suppose that El-Sayed does lose by a few tenths of a point. FLIPR doesn’t have him as that much of a favorite, and it’s probabilistic, but I’ll be honest that this is one of the “misses” that I’d feel relatively less bad about. FLIPR isn’t really equipped to handle late-breaking news that’s too late to show up in the polls. And our midterms model is generally less aggressive than our presidential one, which did move fairly aggressively against Clinton after the Comey news, for instance. So there’s a risk factor here that FLIPR is basically not capturing. I’m not going to manually intervene and subtract seven-tenths of a point from AES’s forecast or something like that.

Not that it’s your duty to care about FLIPR; that’s my job. What’s more important is the impact on the 2028 Democratic primary, where Michigan was already the most narrative-defining race. Now if El-Sayed loses, or wins but significantly underperforms Jocelyn Benson’s margin in the governor’s race or other partisan benchmarks for Michigan, progressives will have a ready-made excuse: Haley Stevens. They might even point to polls showing AES was on track for a clearer win before the endorsement.

This might be a dubious claim. If he loses, the polls might have been wrong all along, and El-Sayed was probably on track to underperform Benson anyway. But this was setting up as one of the cleanest tests in recent memory of whether progressives really do underperform moderates. Now the outcome is confounded. Maybe not hopelessly confounded: we’ll be able to look at things like how late-deciding voters made their minds up in exit polls and whether there was more D-to-R crossover voting than in other states. But confounded enough that moderates won’t be able to make quite as clean an argument if AES underperforms, especially since Democratic Party infighting tends to follow Calvinball rules anyway. Meanwhile, if AES wins by anything more than a point or two, he’ll look more formidable and Stevens and the establishment will look feckless.

A nerdy chat about the midterms

For those of you who want even more Silver Bulletin content, I figured it was worth posting the chat I had on Thursday with Galen Druke and Lakshya Jain of The Argument. Since part of our inspiration was to test out the tech for Tuesday night, this has mild “public access TV” vibes at times, but I think it was a good and substantive conversation that most of you will appreciate.

And we hope to see you Tuesday night — and before then. We’ll be posting FLIPR’s final forecast very early Tuesday morning, and should have another article or two for you in the meantime.

For full access to FLIPR and our Election Night liveblog, please consider becoming a paid subscriber.

1

Full disclosure: if for some reason the liveblog isn’t working, we’ll probably paywall the livestream too.

2

For what it’s worth, I think this is possibly wrong; Silver Bulletin posts that go up on weekends don’t show any meaningful underperformance relative to weekday ones.

3

It was a very late night and I’d played a lot of poker that day.

4

Technically, not all of these voters are undecided per se. FLIPR also lumps in voters for minor third-party candidates that we don’t model explicitly in this column.

5

I suppose my implicit presumption here is that the endorsement won’t flip many El-Sayed voters to Rogers (or vice versa) and that the impact will mostly be felt among undecideds. An actual vote flip costs twice as much as an undecided voter choosing a candidate.

6

I’d contrast this with the stories about operatives associated with Peltola recruiting other Dan Sullivans to be on Alaska’s ballot. Voters might not care about this much, but for the ones who do, it’s almost certain to be directionally negative for Peltola.

item.title: How to judge an election model
item.description: What would it mean for FLIPR to have a bad night? Plus, more on Haley Stevens and those NYT polls in Still Counting EP9.
item.content:encoded:
One more newsletter for you before we publish our final FLIPR forecast shortly after midnight. If you’re new here, we do not usually post this much: it’s typically ~3 items a week, not three a day. But we hope you’ll join us for our final flurry of coverage, including our Election Night livestream and live blog tomorrow.

Subscribe now

And we have a bonus episode of Still Counting out:

Reviews, comments, likes and subscribes are always greatly appreciated. Audio version here:

The context

We covered a lot of ground on the show. But I wrote about those NYT polls and Haley Stevens yesterday, so I’m going to use this as an excuse to cover another topic that Galen, Clare and I were only able to scratch the surface of. I thought it would be nice to write about this ahead of time so it doesn’t feel like spin if a lot of FLIPR’s forecasts don’t come true.

I’ll sometimes get the question, “How do you know if a probabilistic forecast is ever really wrong?” which is an entirely reasonable thing to ask. In fact, let me give you a four-part answer. It’s certainly not quite as simple as saying “30 percent chances are supposed to happen 30 percent of the time.” That’s true insofar as it goes, but it’s incomplete. And if you’re being Bayesian about it, you can’t always use this as a get-of-of-jail-free card. A 0.03 percent chance happening is much more suspect for your model than a 30 percent hitting.

First, the canonical way to answer this. You want your probabilistic forecasts to be well-calibrated over a sufficiently large sample of true out-of-sample predictions. In other words, if you’ve forecasted 100 events that you said had a 30 percent probability of happening, and 27 of them or 34 of them actually did “hit”, your model is doing well.

The “true out-of-sample predictions” part of the answer is important. Backtesting doesn’t count. Any halfway-competently-designed model should fit the past data well; that’s the easy part. But the model may be misfit or overfit, keying off of essentially random factoids in past data that have no true predictive power and aren’t likely to repeat themselves. You may have noticed that in documenting our models, we tend to not make claims like “ELWAY would have gotten the exact score right in the Super Bowl XVI” or “FLIPR would have nailed the 1994 midterm.” Who cares. We already know what happened. I generally think it’s a negative sign when forecasters brag about their backtested results instead of explaining why they think their models make structural sense.

In the case of the Silver Bulletin/FiveThirtyEight lineage of models, however, we have something fairly unique: an 18-year-track record of making true out-of-sample predictions in advance of elections and sporting events, which were published ahead of time, and indeed have received a ton of public scrutiny. At FiveThirtyEight, we actually had an interactive that diligently tracked our forecasts (although the Internet Archive version of the interactive is a little hinky and Disney nuked the original version). Our sports forecasts were extremely well-calibrated: over a large sample size, the 30 percent chances really did hit about 30 percent of the time, and so on. Our politics forecasts were pretty well-calibrated too, although actually a bit underconfident: there were actually too few upsets relative to what our models expected. It’s hard to know whether this is a statistically significant differential1, but it makes me a bit less worried when FLIPR is more confident about a race than the consensus.

For full access to FLIPR, ELWAY, and our other models, please consider becoming a paid subscriber.

A second way is a very Nate way that some of you won’t care for. Would the model have made you money if you’d been betting on it — relative to other models, the conventional wisdom as far as it can be sussed out, or betting markets? If you trusted our model in 2016, you should actually have made a large bet on Trump, because you could get roughly 5-1 or 6-1 odds when our model thought he’d win around 1 time in 3 instead.

We could get into a more detailed discussion about things like Brier scores — you not only want your model to be well-calibrated, you also want it to discriminate clearly between relatively more and relatively less likely outcomes. You’ll be calibrated perfectly if you always forecast every race as 50/50 but the model doesn’t tell you anything.

But I actually think some of the most important ways to evaluate a model are qualitative.

The third thing I always look at is whether a model responds proportionally to new evidence. If either the magnitude or certainly the direction of changes in our model doesn’t pass a common-sense test in accordance with the new evidence, that’s often a sign it’s poorly constructed.

For instance, when that set of very strong NYT/Siena polls for Democrats came out last night, their win probability in the Senate improved by about 2 percentage points in FLIPR. That seems fairly rational. Our odds for Democrats were already pretty favorable. And the NYT/Siena polls have generally been on the higher side of the averages for Dems, so FLIPR was expecting some relatively good numbers. Still, they’re a highly rated pollster, and their polls weren’t just good for Democrats but great in some states like Michigan, often showing favorable trendlines.

By the way, you can also kind of combine #2 and #3. Here, for instance, are Democrats’ Senate odds this year in FLIPR as compared to Polymarket:

This doesn’t always happen, but FLIPR has been leading Polymarket this year, you might notice. They’re going to wind up in roughly the same place, but FLIPR got there faster. Although I know this is self-serving, I’d argue that’s already a little bit of a “W” for FLIPR. (You could, in principle, have bought Democratic positions and sold/hedged them now to lock in a profit.)

Fourth and finally, you should make some effort to determine whether your model was lucky or good. This is sometimes easier in sports. With the Denver Broncos under Bo Nix, for instance, there have been some cases where ELWAY won its bet, but the team really had no business winning the game.

FLIPR has various hypotheses. Just to take a random few:

  • The incumbency advantage matters less than it once did.

  • State-by-state polling errors are correlated in midterms but not as much as in presidential years.

  • Gubernatorial races are less partisan than Congressional ones and produce more crossover voting.

Testable evidence for all of this exists in any given set of election results. If candidate quality matters less than FLIPR expects, maybe Ken Paxton and Roger Marshall hold on. If it matters more, though, maybe they lose but Susan Collins wins.

For all of this, by the way, margins ought to matter and not just the final calls. We’re quite skeptical about Democrats’ chances in Louisiana, for instance, but if Jamie Davis loses by just 1 point, that’s probably a bad forecast and not a good one even though our “call” will be right.

Conversely, some GOP Senate wins would be much worse for FLIPR than others. If Democrats pick up three Senate seats but lose recounts in Texas and Alaska, that’s much closer to FLIPR’s central distribution than if Roy Cooper loses North Carolina.

Possible FLIPR changes and improvements

What sort of things will we be looking to evaluate and potentially change in FLIPR and our other election models? Here are some things I’ve at least thought about. I always think it’s helpful to keep a mental list of these ahead of time so you’re not too overly driven by results and wind up fighting the last war.

  1. Whether to treat polling errors as being somewhat persistent, e.g., Susan Collins should get a boost because she beat her polls last time around.

  2. As discussed in SBSQ, whether to apply some sort of fancier adjustment for undecided voters, i.e., undecideds are presumed to be blue in Minnesota but red in Kansas.

  3. Whether to account for WAR or past election margins for non-incumbents; currently we’re only doing this for incumbents.

  4. Whether to include sources of fundraising other than individual contributions. Currently, we only include individual contributions and not things like PAC money. The individual dollars have been very lopsided in favor of Democrats this year, while the corporate and VIP money has gone the other way.

  5. Whether there’s some feasible way to account for candidate ideology in our “fundamentals” ratings. Currently, we only do this for incumbents, and it’s not really based on ideology per se but rather party loyalty in Congressional voting records.2

  6. Whether improvements could be made in our statewide partisanship scores, like accounting for the differences between midterm and presidential electorates, or changes in voter registration or migration patterns.

  7. Whether to remove the expert ratings layer from FLIPR Deluxe.

  8. Whether to force our estimate of the national House popular vote to more closely match our generic ballot numbers — currently, there’s a difference of about 1 or 1.5 points between these. This is intentional, not a bug, but it’s something we might examine if Democrats considerably outperform their popular vote forecast.

  9. Whether to account for early voting somehow.

  10. And this would be the big one if polls have a bad night: whether generally to de-emphasize polling in favor of other factors, and how that would be implemented, exactly.

But in each case, there’s at least some reason that we aren’t doing these things already. #5 and #6 would be nice, and probably helpful, but it’s not necessarily easy to find the right data, especially if we also need it for lots of past elections to help validate the model. I have a fairly strong prior against #1. For #4, the individual contributions data is nice to have as one of the relatively few objective non-polling inputs in FLIPR. Incorporating early-voting data (#9) would be a beast. It’s a moving target, and you’d need a lot of state-by-state customization; it might take months to do right.

Still, I do try to look at whether the sort of reasonable changes we could make but haven’t made systematically tend to favor one party or the other. Changes #1, #2, #4 and #10 would probably help Republicans this year. But changes #3, #5, #8 and #9 would likely help Democrats. It looks pretty even to me. I was slightly more worried when our model was more D than the consensus, but now prediction markets and other models have mostly converged toward FLIPR.

Of course, #10 is arguably as important as the other nine combined. FLIPR has actually moved slightly in the direction of being more fundamentals-based given the changes we made this summer. But it’s a bit truer to the polls than some of our competitors’ models, especially in estimating the national environment. However, models that make stronger assumptions about fundamentals and let them override polls are easy to overfit, and frankly have a middling-to-poor track record. Nor is it necessarily clear that this would help Republicans anyway, so maybe I was too quick to put #10 in their bucket. As I’ll argue in our closing story, there is lots of non-polling evidence supporting a strong year for Democrats too.

Silver Bulletin news and notes

  • Join us for our Election Night coverage!

  • And so you know, we are updating ELWAY, it just got bumped down the homepage with all of our politics coverage this week.

1

It’s complicated to calculate because polling errors are correlated from state to state, which isn’t true for, say, two NFL games on opposite sides of the country.

2

Other things being equal, candidates who break with their parties more often, like Collins, tend to overperform.

item.title: After an extraordinary wave, what comes next?
item.description: The “smart” conventional wisdom is: midterms don’t predict future elections. I’m not sure about that for a profoundly unpopular lame duck.
item.content:encoded:
We’d like to extend another word of thanks for following FLIPR, our midterm election coverage, and our liveblog last night. We’re really pleased with how everything went, and I can’t express how much more fulfilling it is to run our own business than to work for a big, careless corporation.

I do need to catch up on rest after we published seven stories, plus the liveblog, within a three-day window. That’s not typical for us; we aim for something more like three newsletters per week, plus regularly updating a host of models and statistical tools. Nor are those all politics posts; we also regularly cover sports, AI and sometimes some “wild card” topics. (To control what types of emails appear in your inbox, see here.)

I’m also aware that one can go overboard on post-election recriminations: I think we probably did that in 2024, for instance. On our agenda for the year ahead: rebuilding RAPTOR (our NBA model) and possibly extending PELE, our soccer model, to European club football; beginning our coverage of the 2028 presidential election (sorry, not sorry), probably including some polling tools; expanding our coverage of AI; and a site redesign. We also may be doing some hiring.

Subscribe now

Still, last night’s results deserve deeper consideration than most elections.

As measured by the change in the House popular vote, they featured the second-biggest midterm swing since World War II, which should be around 15 points toward Democrats once all votes are counted.

Democrats will gain 7 to 9 Senate seats — Alaska and Mississippi are pending — along with flipping around 45 House seats and, once all votes are counted in Kansas, probably 6 governorships. Unlike some recent Democratic maps that were concentrated in smaller coastal states, these occurred broadly in basically every corner of the country. (Well, except Florida, as usual.) Once new terms begin, Democrats will control the governorships in states totaling around three-quarters of the U.S. population; in the Electoral College, this would translate to a 392-146 landslide.1

There were plenty of signature wins too. Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Kansas since 1932. Not only did James Talarico win by double digits in Texas; Gina Hinojosa flipped the governorship there. Keisha Lance Bottoms became the nation’s first Black female governor. They won a Senate seat in South Carolina, and if prediction markets are right, they’ll flip Mississippi too. The repudiation that Democrats have been waiting 10 years for against Donald Trump finally came, and bigly.

Friend-of-the-newsletter Sean Trende has written that this was a “100-year flood”, the usual nomenclature of waves and tsunamis not quite sufficing. There are deep implications for the future of the Democratic Party, the Republican Party and the Supreme Court, and we’ll be covering all of that. Polls (and models) also had a lot on the line, although the results take some care to interpret. On the one hand, the results back up our theory that the direction of polling bias is unpredictable; on the other hand, it was a pretty big and broad lowballing of Democrats.

But let’s keep today’s post relatively simple. I’ll look at what happened after other waves of roughly this magnitude. This is the seventh time since World War II that a midterm featured a swing of 10 points or more; the others were 1946, 1966, 1974, 1994, 2006 and 2010. For each one, I’ll ask a few simple questions: what caused the wave, how similar it is to this year, and most importantly, what came next.

As I expressed to Ezra Klein before the election, this midterm felt “momentous” because it potentially reflects the end of the Trump Era and the transition into … well, who knows what. But two years ago, everyone was talking about a conservative “vibe shift”, and that obviously didn’t pan out.

1946 (13.2-point swing)

When it happened: During Harry Truman’s first (unelected) term.

Outcome: Republicans gained 55 House seats, 12 Senate seats and 3 governorships.

Why it happened:

  • An abrupt shift from the wartime to the peacetime economy, which had produced a recession in 1945, followed by supply-chain shortages, high inflation and strikes;

  • Truman’s lower stature as compared to FDR and his low popularity ratings;

  • Perhaps pent-up backlash toward Democrats and lots of viable targets after four consecutive FDR terms.

What happened next: Truman upset Thomas Dewey in 1948, and Democrats made unusually large gains in Congress for a presidential year, basically fully reversing their 1946 losses. However, Truman was unpopular for much of his second term. Not officially a lame duck — the 22nd Amendment exempted him — he stood down after considering a third term in 1952, and Dwight D. Eisenhower won in a landslide.

Did it mark the end of an era/beginning of a new one? Politically speaking? I’d argue no. The end of World War II was a huge inflection point for the world, of course, and marked the emergence of the United States as a hegemonic superpower. But when I’ve covered this in the past, I consider everything from 1932 through 1968 to be part of “The Long Liberal Era”, with FDR and LBJ ushering in the New Deal and Great Society, respectively. Eisenhower was a notably moderate Republican, meanwhile, in an era of high bipartisan comity.

Applicability to 2026: If you follow politics, you’ll have a direct memory of some elections. The first one I remember watching — really just fragments, flickers of Reagan’s dominant map on the network newscasts — was in 1984. But the elections your parents remember will also be part of the “training set”: the collective memory that shapes conventional wisdom about how elections work. 1946 came before either of those, and that probably biases me against wanting to think it’s particularly relevant to today. You can draw some parallels: is the emergence of AI like the end of the war? And pent-up fatigue: Trump hasn’t had three terms in a row, but it feels like he has. Overall, this seems like a stretch.

1966 (12-point swing)

Outcome: Republicans gained 47 House seats and 3 Senate seats, although they failed to take control of either chamber; they also added 8 governorships, mostly west of the Mississippi.

When it happened: During LBJ’s second — but first elected — term. Like Truman, he therefore wasn’t a true lame duck, but dropped out of the 1968 race after a close call in the New Hampshire primary that was treated as a vote of no confidence.

Why it happened:

  • Increasing opposition to the Vietnam War on the left;

  • Increasing opposition to the Civil Rights movement and the hippies on the right;

  • Republicans were starting from a very, very low floor during a period in which they routinely got trounced in elections to Congress;

  • LBJ had brought sweeping changes to the welfare state.

What happened next? 1968 was competitive, with Hubert H. Humphrey nearly winning the popular vote, but Nixon was re-elected in a landslide in 1972. Overall, Republicans won the presidency in 5 of 6 elections, excepting only 1976.

Did it mark the end of an era/beginning of a new one? Yes, I’d say: I think it was the precursor to the transition from the Long Liberal Era to the Long Conservative Era.

Applicability to 2026: Well, there’s a parallel in the form of a stupid war that nobody was asking for. And although LBJ wasn’t constitutionally a lame duck, he was on his back heel. But in other ways, the comparison is weaker. LBJ really did have an enormous mandate after his landslide in 1964, something that Trump never did.

1974 (11.2-point swing)

Outcome: Democrats gained 45 House seats, developing an enormous majority, along with 4 Senate seats and 4 governorships.

When it happened: Amid Gerald Ford’s lone (unelected) term after Nixon resigned the presidency in August 1974 following Watergate.

Why it happened: Watergate and inflation.

What happened next? A dark-horse Democratic nominee, Jimmy Carter, only narrowly beat Ford before losing in a landslide to Ronald Reagan in 1980 in an election that also produced massive gains in Congress for Republicans.

Did it mark the end of an era/beginning of a new one? No. Carter was not exactly transformational, and his presidency looks like a blip in the Long Conservative Era.

Applicability to 2026: People love this one, citing corruption and the high cost of living as parallels. And although Ford wasn’t a lame duck, Nixon had been and, like Trump, had been a central political figure for a long time, having been elected vice president in 1952. But I’d argue it’s only a medium-good comp. 1974 had a relatively singular cause, and scandals don’t bother the American public in the way they once did; corruption might have been only third on the list of voter concerns about Trump after high gas prices and Iran.

1994 (12.1-point swing)

Outcome: Republicans picked up 54 House seats, 8 Senate seats, and 10 governorships.

When it happened: In Bill Clinton’s first term, after he’d won in 1992 with a strong Electoral College performance but not a majority of the popular vote.

Why it happened:

  • The Clintons’ overreach on Hillarycare;

  • Bill Clinton’s personal scandals;

  • Although Clinton’s agenda wasn’t radical, we were in the midst of the Long Conservative Era;

  • Clinton had a tenuous mandate. Although he became popular following 1994, his first-term numbers more closely resembled the 43 percent of the vote he was elected with against George H.W. Bush and Ross Perot;

  • This was one of several elections (also 1972, 2010, 2016) that marked a series of step changes against Democrats in the rural South.

What happened next? Clinton performed a hard pivot to the center and was re-elected easily, although again without a popular-vote majority. His vice president, Al Gore, won the popular vote but lost the Electoral College to George W. Bush despite Clinton’s popularity and a strong economy.

Did it mark the end of an era/beginning of a new one? For me, no. Clinton was a centrist and triangulating president, which is why I see his presidency as being part of the Long Conservative Era.

Applicability to 2026: It’s a stretch. Clinton was in his first term, and although you can argue he overread his mandate, this ranks higher than most waves on structural explanations. The Democrats’ “Solid South” was falling apart and partisanship began a sharp rise under Newt Gingrich.

2006 (10.6 points)

Outcome: Democrats netted 31 House seats, flipped 6 Republican-held Senate seats (winning both chambers) and gained 6 governor’s mansions.

When it happened: In George Bush’s second, lame-duck term, following a close re-election in 2004.

Why it happened:

  • Bush’s ever-declining popularity amid fatigue with the War on Terror, his mishandling of Hurricane Katrina and his failed attempt at Social Security reform.

  • Bush governing as if he had a huge mandate when 2004 had been close.

  • Republican corruption and scandals.

  • Arguably, early warning signs of the mortgage bubble.

What happened next? Bush’s popularity continued to plummet; instead, the Republican nominee was John McCain, a Bush critic. But McCain nevertheless lost to Barack Obama by 7+ points, and Democrats had another huge year in Congress to rack up massive majorities in both chambers of Congress.

Did it mark the end of an era/beginning of a new one? Clearly yes; I consider 2006 to be basically the end of the Long Conservative Era and the start of the New Liberal Era under Obama and later Biden.

Applicability to 2026: Obviously quite high. You had basically the same ingredients: unpopular wars, unforced errors, and looming economic anxiety. It’s also the only true lame duck midterm on the list. I’ve argued before that there are sharp parallels between 2004 and 2024, including the media being convinced that America was a “center-right country” despite the narrowness of the Bush and Trump wins. And take a look at this comparison between Bush and Trump’s second-term approval ratings:

2010 (17.4 points)

Outcome: Republicans hit the jackpot, picking up 6 Senate seats, 6 governorships, and 63 House seats.

When it happened: During Barack Obama’s first term, following his landslide win in 2008.

Why it happened:

  • The weak economic recovery following the global financial crisis and persistently high unemployment;

  • Democrats had a broad list of targets to defend after consecutive landslides in 2006 and 2008, with particular exposure in rural districts where the demographics were turning against them;

  • They had charged ahead to pass Obamacare even after losing a special Senate election in Massachusetts;

  • Populist backlash was brewing amid the rise of the Tea Party, which now reads like a precursor to Trumpism;

  • Obama’s penchant for turning out younger, low-propensity voters, particularly minorities, worked out well in presidential years but poorly in midterms.

What happened next? Obama, in a well-executed campaign, rebounded to soundly defeat Mitt Romney, picking up 2 Senate seats in the process to bolster the Democratic majority but failing to flip the House. A turnout/enthusiasm gap was again a problem for him in 2014 amidst a tepid economy, but he left office as a relatively popular president by modern standards. But then Democrats nominated Hillary Clinton, and then came Trump.

Did it mark the end of an era/beginning of a new one? Not really. In some ways, it was kind of the reverse; this election was more of a market correction amid an emerging liberal era. Democrats would go on to win the popular vote for the U.S. presidency three more times in a row, with Obama’s vice president, Joe Biden, winning the Electoral College as a 77-year-old in 2020. But 2006/2008 only partly reflected a vibe shift involving changing cultural values on issues like gay marriage; there were also a lot of contingencies related to Bush, which didn’t have as much resonance once he was out of office, kept a low profile and tried his hand at painting.

Applicability to 2026: Strong in the sense that it’s the only swing of the same magnitude. But overall, relatively weak. Obama was in his first term, and had a far bigger mandate than Trump. Ironically, the parties have now swapped positions, and it was Trump who relied on low-propensity voters in his two Electoral College wins in 2016 and 2024 but has performed poorly in other elections.

So what can we learn from this?

Well, that’s not so straightforward.

Some experts have claimed that the predictive power of midterms is basically zero when forecasting forthcoming elections. (In fact, I’m guilty as charged; we published one such analysis at FiveThirtyEight.)

And it’s true that if you build a scatterplot of the magnitude of the midterm wave on the x-axis, and subsequent election results on the y-axis, it looks more or less random.

I have three critiques of this, though. One is a minor quibble: most midterms are waves, but analyses of elections like 2026 ought to focus on the ones that are similar in magnitude to it. With that said, there’s not much obvious signal: 2010 didn’t end up being all that bad for Barack Obama and Democrats, and even the public backlash to Watergate in 1974 didn’t persist for very long.

The second is that people tend to focus solely on the results of the next election two years later when long-term shifts are probably more important.

The main critique, however, is that these past midterm waves are very unlike one another. There are some common ingredients in play — overreaching one’s mandate, high exposure due to past success, dumb wars, etc. But the ratios are slightly different from election to election. In some cases, structural changes are a strong factor, and in others they don’t matter at all. In some years, like this one and in 1946, the president is extremely unpopular; in others, he’s only somewhat unpopular and the issue is more that there’s a relative decline from an election that brought large coattails.

The one crystal-clear parallel — I’d argue more than 1974 — is 2006, the only true lame-duck election on the list. That produced another landslide against Republicans two years later.

Am I just cherry-picking here? Yeah, kind of. Unfortunately, we sometimes have to do that in election analysis since we don’t get very many data points. I suppose my prior is that if we had 60 past elections instead of six, you would see some signal. But the point is, I think you’re allowed to be a little more qualitative when you don’t have enough reliable data points to fit a model anyway.

And one factor to consider is: how in the hell are Republicans going to go about picking an appealing candidate for 2028? JD Vance is the leader in prediction markets, but he’s Trump’s vice president. Marco Rubio, the other frontrunner, is the Secretary of State. I’m not sure there’s any John McCain looming on the horizon because it’s hard to be a McCain in Trump’s version of the Republican Party, which constantly excommunicates dissenters.

So really my argument is this. It seems unlikely to me that Trump’s approval rating, currently 38 percent, is liable to get all that much better. The decline in his numbers over the past two years has been remarkably persistent, instead. Plus, he’s 80 years old, and doesn’t seem to care about the implications of his unpopularity for anyone else in the Republican Party. I don’t think anyone is expecting him to attempt a Clintonian pivot, much less to pull it off. And the Republican nominee in 2028 will have to navigate an incredibly treacherous tightrope: distancing themselves just enough from Trump without triggering his ire. This produced a massive fail for Ron DeSantis last time around.

Until last night, you could at least argue that Trump’s low popularity was a mirage, a reflection of polls that weren’t capturing his real supporters. But not only did Republicans lose Senate seats in Texas (!) and South Carolina (!!) and Kansas (!!!) and maybe Mississippi (!!!!): Democrats were considerably underestimated by the polls. One theory for the polling miss, ironically, is that Trump is so unpopular that respondents won’t admit they once supported him, which can inflate Republican results in surveys that weight to past vote recall.

So, we’ll see. Democrats have plenty of their own problems, and last night didn’t erase them. We’re in an era when most presidential elections are close. I just don’t think you can witness last night without recognizing that Republicans are in a hell of a predicament. I’ll have more to say about this soon.

item.title: Models led prediction markets in forecasting the blue wave
item.description: But who deserves the most credit? High-quality pollsters who nailed the result. Plus, Still Counting EP10.
item.content:encoded:
Our weekly episode of Still Counting is ready. This was taped yesterday morning, so you can blame any bad takes on sleep deprivation:

And here’s the audio. We’re very grateful for any reviews, comments, likes and subscribes. Yes, I’m going to say that every week.

The context

Despite results on Tuesday that, to a first approximation, made our coverage this year look smart, Clare, Galen and I were all in slightly different moods. Elections build up to a stressful crescendo, frankly. It’s in the final days when you both have the most on the line and the most to do.

Subscribe now

And we’re still feeling that stress, to some extent. So rather than come up with the perfect transition paragraph, I’m going to semi-awkwardly pivot to a debate about models versus prediction markets.1

I don’t particularly like this debate. To a large extent, I think of pollsters, modelers, prediction markets and smart political wonks as all being within “the industry”. Their interests are mostly aligned with one another. And sometimes they’re aligned against the conventional wisdom or the media ecosystem more broadly.

If you’ve read the book, it’s kind of a Village vs. River thing. Or smart money vs. dumb money. The smart money was on Democrats having a good and possibly great election. The smart money doesn’t always get it right, though.

Still, I’m finding myself a little annoyed if prediction markets are trying to take a disproportionate share of the credit as opposed to “the industry” broadly. A few key points.

FLIPR was — correctly, given what happened — more confident in overall Democratic odds in the Senate throughout the stretch run of the campaign.2

For the Nov. 3 datapoint in this chart, I’m using the last “print” of prediction market data before any results were reported starting at 6 p.m. There was a weird little jitter back toward Republicans at prediction markets during the course of the day on Tuesday, which was directionally wrong and I don’t think had any real basis, as I wrote at the time. Prediction markets are smart about incorporating new information, and in principle that’s one of their advantages versus models — we have to wait for whatever happens to show up in the polls. At the same time, there’s sometimes a “buy the rumor, sell the news” thing going on here. Markets almost certainly overreacted to the Haley Stevens thing in Michigan and to random reports about turnout on Tuesday morning and afternoon.

Once results began to come in on Tuesday, prediction markets very, very quickly honed in on the right results. They were better than the networks, and faster than the NYT Needle. That was impressive, though I think we got to the right answer pretty quickly in the liveblog, too.

However, if we are going to turn this into a competition, I think the better models like FLIPR unambiguously had a better pre-election period. Our model arrived at the right answer faster, leading the markets by days to weeks.

Indeed, our forecasts moved the markets when they launched on Aug. 11. This is as clear an indication as you can get that traders believe we provide alpha that the markets alone are not capturing.

Furthermore, prediction market probabilities strongly converged toward ours in individual Senate and gubernatorial races. I was tracking this stuff closely, precisely because I envisioned that we might wind up in this sort of debate where prediction markets are low-key stealing valor from the models. I grabbed these prices late Tuesday morning. First for the Senate:

And then for gubernatorial races:

The differences are interesting. In the Nevada governor’s race, for instance, prediction markets were clearly incorporating some assumptions about early voting in correctly being more confident about Aaron Ford than we were. I think that was smart, although that’s partly because early-voting analysis tends to be unusually reliable in Nevada as compared to other states.

Sometimes, I have subjective takes that might override FLIPR, but we think projects like FLIPR are going to be more informative in the long run if we stick to the algorithm.

I am interested in the differences, however. I discussed the Senate races where prediction markets and FLIPR disagreed in a post on Oct. 25. The funny thing was, in several of the races like South Carolina, FLIPR was more accurate, but my “gut” was on the wrong side of FLIPR! Prediction markets do deserve some credit relative to FLIPR on Mississippi, though, where Scott Colom is probably going to win in a major upset.

Overall, though, prediction market prices converged toward FLIPR, and not the other way around. Here were the prices as of Oct. 25:

You can see that there were some bigger gaps then than we wound up with on Tuesday. Although, the correlation was >=.99 in both cases.

You can also debate how to compare them. If Peltola wins in Alaska but by an underwhelming margin, as seems likely, does FLIPR deserve credit for showing a closer race? Or not, because prediction markets also “called” the right winner, but did so more confidently? Any evaluation that anyone publishes is usually going to be low-key biased toward the most favorable “reasonable” method for their forecast.

In the end, prediction markets and the better models converged on basically the same prices. But as you can see by comparing the Oct. 25 graphic to the Nov. 3 graphic, prediction markets moved toward model prices and not the other way around. The prices they wound up with on Tuesday morning, we often had days to weeks sooner.

I don’t want to turn this into a competition between Silver Bulletin and the other models. Split Ticket and FiftyPlusOne in particular also have smart models. (There’s more or less a “right” way to build one of these, so we all use pretty similar approaches.) Different analyses put their performance in slightly different orders. Yes, there were one or two other models that I thought were slightly wacky, but in general, these differences have dissipated, and the modeling part of “the industry” has matured from, say, 2016.

But traders get to use our forecasts, and they trust them, and I’m sure they make up some proportion of our subscription business.

The best-performing models, including FLIPR, don’t use prediction market data, however. They provide truly independent information. If there aren’t reliable models to look at, prediction markets are still often smart. But they can also get unhinged, like in the Wisconsin and Michigan Democratic primaries this year.

Building these models is a lot of work, with some subtle dynamics that take a lot of time to explore fully. One of those, for instance, is that polling in primaries is much less accurate than polls of general elections. So the markets sometimes wind up trusting polls too much in primaries, and too little in general elections.

It’s flattering that traders tend to trust our prices. But in a world where these models didn’t exist, or if the models kept their forecasts private, I don’t think the prediction markets would be as accurate on either an absolute or relative basis.

However, there’s an irony here. Just like the prediction markets are downstream of the models and benefit from their existence, the models are downstream from the inputs they use, including the polls. If you ask me, who really deserves the most credit is pollsters like NYT/Siena and AtlasIntel that provided highly accurate results that defied the consensus to some degree. There would have been hell to pay if these polls had been off, especially given that the president has sued pollsters before that he didn’t like. It showed some courage for them to stick their necks out there and they deserve a victory lap.

So if I had to rank-order this, I’d go something like:

1) NYT, AtlasIntel and other high-quality pollsters who trusted their own data and published their results at some risk of embarrassment.

Close 2nd) The better models, including but not limited to FLIPR.

Close 3rd) Prediction markets. They did have a good year, certainly. And I think it shows them maturing that they increasingly trust the more reliable sources of information and shut out the noise.

Distant 4th) The conventional wisdom, more broadly, which incorrectly assumed that polls are persistently biased against Republicans. They aren’t. Polling bias is basically random from cycle to cycle, in part because pollsters adjust their methods in response to errors. This election wasn’t the first time that polls missed low on Democrats. The same thing happened in the New Jersey and Virginia gubernatorial races last year, and in the presidential election of 2012.

Silver Bulletin news and notes

  • Clare, Galen and I will be at Crooked Con in Washington D.C. this weekend, with a live Still Counting episode at 9 a.m. on Saturday!

  • The post-election period can be tricky. As discussed yesterday, we’re going to look to strike a balance between reflections on the midterm, more forward-looking coverage, and posts that have nothing to do with the election at all. We have a big year planned, including one or two new sports model launches. We also need to get some rest.

To receive new posts and support our work, please consider becoming a subscriber.

1

I’m an advisor to Polymarket. But my first priority is always the newsletter, and saying what I think, including when prediction markets get things wrong.

2

And to a lesser extent in the House, although everyone was highly confident throughout.
